overview: A ten-minute interactive VR training experience for the Shockwave E8 peripheral IVL catheter. Charles Dotter's original 1964 angioplasty film meets a local-language KOL in a London cinema, then the viewer steps inside a calcified artery to treat it themselves.
body1:
Peripheral intervention started on film. In 1964 Charles Dotter performed the first percutaneous transluminal angioplasty and filmed it himself. He wrote, narrated and often shot his own teaching films, and he called the technique "Dottering".

Shockwave asked us to build a VR training experience for the E8 peripheral IVL catheter, to take to physicians at Charing Cross and beyond. We saw a way to put Dotter's footage to work: let the man who founded the field set out the problem, then let a physician today show where it has led.

The result is Dottering to Shocking, a ten-minute interactive experience in English, German, Italian and Spanish. A KOL from each market sits in an old London cinema, watches Dotter's 1964 film with the viewer, then takes them inside a real patient's calcified artery to treat it with IVL.
body2:
Calcium has been the hard problem in peripheral intervention for as long as there has been peripheral intervention. The brief came with a few challenges of its own.

One story, four markets. Each market needed a presenter its physicians would recognise as their own, speaking their own language, rather than an English film with subtitles.

Archive footage in a headset. Dotter's film is grainy, scratched and sixty years old. It had to sit alongside 360 live action and real-time 3D without feeling like a museum piece.

A mechanism you can feel. Physicians know the theory of IVL. We wanted them to stand inside a rigid, non-compliant vessel, position the catheter, inflate the balloon and deliver the pulses with their own hands.

Sizing that sticks. Angiography alone can underestimate vessel diameter, and an undersized balloon undertreats the calcium. That message had to live inside the interaction, not on a slide.

Built for the congress floor. It had to load onto a fleet of headsets, run without a technician and fit a ten-minute slot on a busy stand.
body3:
We shot at the Electric Cinema on Portobello Road. Each KOL was filmed on their own in 360, speaking to camera in their own language with Dotter's film playing on the screen behind them.

The story is one case told twice. In 1964, Dotter's patient Burt limps across a road with a narrowed superficial femoral artery. Today, Peter is a retired chef born the year Dotter made his film, now facing chronic limb-threatening ischaemia. The film moves between the two through patient history, imaging, device set-up and outcome, with Dotter's original narration carrying his half.

The VR chapters take the viewer inside Peter's artery, built from his CT data, with live IVUS and fluoroscopy displays tracking the headset. The user grabs the E8 catheter and finds the lesion, guided by haptic feedback in the controller. They size and inflate the balloon, then trigger each pulse and watch microfractures spread through the calcium in real time. A second visit after IVL shows the same vessel with its lumen restored.

In post, the 360 footage was cleaned and graded shot by shot, the four language tracks were mixed, and the films were brought into the interactive build and deployed across the headsets through ManageXR.
body4:
At CIRSE 2026 we handed a short paper survey to people as they took the headset off. Nineteen completed it, a mix of physicians, nurses, trainees, industry and technical staff.

They rated the overall value of the experience 9.1 out of 10, and their likelihood to recommend it to a colleague treating calcified PAD 8.8. Nobody scored either question below 7, and 16 of the 19 gave it a 9 or 10. Every respondent agreed that VR adds educational value beyond traditional formats, with no neutral answers.

The biggest gains were in the most mechanism-specific areas. Around two-thirds said the experience significantly improved their understanding of why calcified vessels limit balloon angioplasty and how IVL may support vessel preparation, and everyone left at least somewhat confident applying what they'd learned to a real calcified PAD decision. Asked what landed most, 16 of 19 named being inside the artery with the lesion, and 11 named experiencing IVL in immersive VR.

Sixty years apart, Burt and Peter were both back on their feet within days. The experience ends with Peter in his kitchen, carrying plates up two steps to his family's table.
